briefDescription: Jordan from Deloitte agreed to a 30-minute informational interview. He has a Google Doc of questions and a genuine desire to help. You need to seem like someone worth helping.
openingLine: Hey! So glad we could make this work — I actually blocked off 45 minutes just in case because I feel like these conversations always go longer than expected, which is a good thing. I want to make sure you get everything you need out of this. I have some thoughts but honestly, tell me a little about yourself first?

dialogueNodes.characterLine: That's really interesting. I feel like a lot of people come into consulting without fully understanding what the day-to-day looks like — it's honestly a lot more spreadsheets and client management than the recruiting materials suggest. What's drawing you specifically to the strategy work versus, like, implementation?

options.text: Honestly, I'm drawn to the problem-solving breadth. I want to be in a room where the question is still being defined, not just executing against a framework someone else built. The strategy-to-implementation handoff is where insight gets lost and I'd rather be upstream of that.
options.characterThinks: He actually said something coherent — I'm going to have to update my canned response.

options.text: I've been thinking about this a lot actually. Strategy without execution is just slide-ware, but I want to build the muscle for structuring ambiguous problems before I specialize. The generalist reps matter early.
options.characterThinks: That's a reasonable answer. Probably practiced it in the mirror but it still landed.

options.text: I mean, the distinction is getting increasingly blurry — most strategic recommendations are worthless if you can't model the implementation constraints. I'm honestly more interested in the data layer than the deck.
options.characterThinks: Okay, data layer, sure. Slightly off but I'll let it breathe.

options.text: I think the strategy vs. implementation binary is itself a bit of a construct? The firms that do well are the ones that don't silo those functions. I'm more interested in working across that false dichotomy.
options.characterThinks: He just called my entire career a construct. We have 38 minutes left.

options.text: Look, I'll be straight — I want to do two years, get the brand on my resume, and move into PE or corp dev. I know that's what half your analysts do. I just want to learn the modeling rigor and the client communication.
options.characterThinks: I appreciate the honesty and I am writing 'exit-oriented' in my notes right now.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: Yeah, totally. I'll be honest with you — the first six months are mostly about learning how to communicate uncertainty to clients without scaring them. There's a lot of 'we're still pressure-testing the hypothesis' language. Have you done any case prep? I don't want to be that person but the interviews are genuinely hard.

options.text: I've been doing cases for about three months — mostly peer practice but I've also done a few with former consultants. My issue right now is synthesizing the recommendation under time pressure. The logic is there but the packaging gets rushed.
options.characterThinks: Okay this person has actually done cases. I can work with this.

options.text: I've done some, but honestly I think the case interview is an imperfect signal. I learn better by doing — I've done more to sharpen my thinking through actual projects than through manufactured airport problem sets.
options.characterThinks: That's a great philosophy that will get you dinged in round one.

options.text: Yes — I've been thinking about case prep as product development, honestly. Each case is a sprint, you're shipping a recommendation with incomplete data. That framing has helped me structure faster.
options.characterThinks: That's a moderately interesting reframe. I'm giving it a 6/10.

options.text: I've been thinking about case prep but also about whether the McKinsey problem-solving framework is actually epistemically sound or just a very expensive way to arrive at the mean.
options.characterThinks: I am going to finish this coffee and end the meeting at 20 minutes.

options.text: Honestly I've been slammed with recruiting across multiple tracks so my case prep is a little behind, but I work well under pressure and I ramp fast — that's been my whole thing.
options.characterThinks: Every person I've met this semester says they 'ramp fast.' The market is saturated.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: Good — yeah, the synthesis piece is really where it clicks or doesn't. Okay, shifting gears a little: what do you want to be doing in five years? I know that's a cliche question but I genuinely find it useful because it tells me what kind of referral to make.

options.text: In five years I want to be at a point where I'm leading client relationships, not just contributing to decks. The goal is to get to engagement manager track, build a functional specialty — probably in ops or org — and then reevaluate from a position of optionality.
options.characterThinks: This is exactly the right answer and I slightly resent how well he's doing this.

options.text: Honestly five years is a long horizon for me right now. I see consulting as a two-year intensive that gets me to a place where I can evaluate what's actually interesting — maybe operator roles, maybe something on the investment side.
options.characterThinks: Everyone wants to 'evaluate optionality' after two years. I was the same. It's fine.

options.text: Honestly? Running something. I want to have built meaningful leverage — either as a founder or an operator — and consulting is how I get exposure to enough industries to figure out where the real opportunity is.
options.characterThinks: Points for ambition. Slight ding for the 'running something' non-answer that every MBA says.

options.text: Honestly, the consulting model might look pretty different in five years given the direction of AI capabilities. I'm interested in consulting as a pattern-recognition accelerant, not as a career track per se.
options.characterThinks: He just told me my job is going away. We have 22 minutes left.

options.text: I think I want to work on things that matter — like climate, or access, or something with real societal impact. I'm exploring whether consulting is the right vehicle for that or if it's more of a detour.
options.characterThinks: He wants to work on things that matter and he's thinking about whether consulting is a detour. Same, buddy. Same.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: That makes sense. I will say — and I tell everyone this — the two-year thing is real but you have to actually commit when you're there. The people who treat it as a layover do worse work and get worse references. Okay, do you have questions for me? I want to make sure you're getting what you need.

options.text: Yeah — I'm curious what surprised you most about the culture after you joined. Not the stuff in the recruiting materials, but the thing that took you a month to calibrate to.
options.characterThinks: That's the best question anyone has asked me in a coffee chat this year. I was not prepared to enjoy this.

options.text: I'd love to understand your mental model for evaluating which projects to volunteer for early on — like how do you build your internal reputation before you have a track record?
options.characterThinks: Good question. Strategic. He's thinking about leverage already. I respect it.

options.text: What's the vibe like in terms of work-life balance? I hear it varies a lot by team and I want to make sure I'm going in with realistic expectations.
options.characterThinks: Work-life balance. The question that launches a thousand vague answers. Here comes mine.

options.text: Real talk — what's the comp trajectory look like from analyst to senior consultant? I want to benchmark against what I'm seeing on IB offers.
options.characterThinks: He's comp-benchmarking me against bankers to my face. Genuinely audacious. I'll answer but I'll remember.

options.text: I actually don't have a ton of questions — I've done a lot of research and feel pretty oriented. I'm more interested in whether you think I'd be a good fit based on what we've talked about.
options.characterThinks: Bold move — putting the evaluation on me. Points for confidence. Slight alarm at the directness.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: Honestly the thing that surprised me most was how much the culture depends on your specific partner — like, my first engagement I had a partner who ran really tight ships and I learned a ton, but my second partner basically ghosted the team. It's very uneven. What's your biggest concern going into the process?

options.text: Honestly, my biggest concern is the fit interview more than the case. I can structure a problem but I'm aware that 'fit' in consulting has a specific texture — calibrated confidence, not just warmth — and I'm still finding my version of that.
options.characterThinks: 'Calibrated confidence, not just warmth.' I need to write that down. This person is good.

options.text: I worry a little that my background reads as unconventional — I didn't take the finance-heavy path and I want to make sure interviewers are seeing the analytical rigor in what I've actually done.
options.characterThinks: Reasonable concern, self-aware, not self-pitying. I can actually help here.

options.text: I think my concern is whether I can stay authentic to my values in a highly commercial environment. I want to do meaningful work and I'm not sure if that's a tension I'll feel early.
options.characterThinks: I have a form I fill out after each coffee chat and one of the fields is 'values tension concerns.' It is always a yellow flag.

options.text: Honestly, not much — I think I can learn case interviewing fast. My bigger meta-concern is whether consulting is the right move given how rapidly the advisory market is getting commoditized by AI tools.
options.characterThinks: He is asking me for help getting into an industry he thinks is dying. The audacity is almost impressive.

options.text: Mostly getting through the quantitative sections cleanly — I can do the math but under pressure I sometimes skip steps in my head and lose the interviewer. I'm drilling that specifically.
options.characterThinks: Self-aware about a specific weakness. That's actually the right answer. Normal good answer.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: That's a really self-aware answer. Okay, I'm going to be honest — you've made a strong impression and I'm happy to pass your name along. But I want to give you one piece of feedback: you want to project conviction. Interviewers here can smell hedging from a mile out. Does that resonate?

options.text: Completely — and honestly that's the exact feedback I needed to hear. I tend to over-qualify my recommendations as a reflex. I'll work on landing stronger conclusions.
options.characterThinks: He just received feedback and immediately integrated it. He's going to be fine.

options.text: Yeah it does. I think I sometimes lead with nuance when I should be leading with the insight. The nuance can follow — the conviction has to be up front.
options.characterThinks: Nice synthesis. He turned my feedback into a framework. Slightly too smooth but I'll allow it.

options.text: Totally resonates. I think I've been optimizing for being seen as thorough over being seen as decisive. Those aren't the same thing and I need to separate them.
options.characterThinks: Solid self-diagnosis. PM-brained but that's not a dealbreaker here.

options.text: Somewhat — I think there's also a version of conviction that reads as incuriosity to certain interviewers though. I try to calibrate to the room.
options.characterThinks: He just pushed back on my feedback. Mid-coffee chat. Bold. Wrong call, but bold.

options.text: I appreciate that. I'd actually push back slightly — I think the industry's preference for performed conviction over epistemic honesty is part of why so many consulting recommendations are confidently wrong.
options.characterThinks: He is arguing with me about the epistemics of conviction while asking me to refer him. The meeting is over.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: Great. I'm going to send you a couple names at McKinsey and BCG too — just to give you options. Last question, and this is just for my own curiosity: why consulting and not tech? Because you seem like someone who'd do well in both.

options.text: Honestly the breadth of exposure early in consulting is hard to replicate — in tech you specialize fast. I want to understand how businesses work at the strategic level before I go deep in any one of them.
options.characterThinks: Perfect answer. I've heard it 200 times and I still believe it every single time.

options.text: Honestly, the overlap is getting larger. I see consulting as a forcing function to develop structured problem-solving rigor that I'd then apply in a more technical context. They're not that different at the problem-framing layer.
options.characterThinks: He's basically saying consulting is a stepping stone to tech. I respect the honesty even though it's a ding.

options.text: I looked at tech but the comp is actually better out of consulting if you're looking at total package and exit multiples over a five-year horizon. People underrate how good the comp is here.
options.characterThinks: He just told me he chose consulting for the exit multiples. I will still refer him. But I'll remember.

options.text: Ultimately I want to build something — consulting gives me a map of the landscape before I decide what to build. Tech would narrow me before I've earned the right to go narrow.
options.characterThinks: He wants to build. Fine. Half of Deloitte wants to build. He'll still be here in three years.

options.text: I actually did consider tech pretty hard. The thing consulting has that most tech companies don't is genuine exposure to messy organizational problems — and I find those more interesting than pure technical problems right now.
options.characterThinks: That's actually a thoughtful answer. He considered the alternative seriously. I like this one.
